Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a district court abuses its discretion in denying a 28 U.S.C. 1404(a) transfer where the transferee venue is clearly more convenient.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The District Court Clearly Abused Its Discretion in Denying Transfer Because the Transferee Venue Is Clearly More Convenient.

#### A. Section 1404(a) requires transfer when the movant shows the transferee forum is clearly more convenient.

Section 1404(a) permits transfer "[f]or the convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice," to any district where the action might have been brought. 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). The movant must show "good cause," which means demonstrating that the transferee venue is "clearly more convenient." *In re Volkswagen of Am., Inc.*, 545 F.3d 304, 315 (5th Cir. 2008) (en banc) (*Volkswagen II*). Although the district court has broad discretion, that discretion is bounded by the governing factors. Denial of transfer is reviewable, and mandamus is appropriate when the court clearly abuses its discretion. *Id.* at 310–12; *In re Volkswagen AG*, 371 F.3d 201, 203 (5th Cir. 2004) (*Volkswagen I*); *see also In re Radmax, Ltd.*, 720 F.3d 285, 287–88 (5th Cir. 2013).

The inquiry weighs four private-interest factors: (1) the relative ease of access to sources of proof; (2) the availability of compulsory process for unwilling witnesses; (3) the cost of attendance for willing witnesses; and (4) other practical problems. It also weighs four public-interest factors: (1) administrative difficulties from court congestion; (2) the local interest in resolving localized disputes; (3) the forum's familiarity with the governing law; and (4) avoiding conflict-of-law problems. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 315; *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 203. A court that misapplies these factors, or gives weight to considerations that do not belong in the analysis, abuses its discretion. *Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 288–90.

#### B. The private- and public-interest factors establish that [Transferee District] is clearly more convenient.

*Sources of proof and witnesses.* The relevant documents, physical evidence, and non-party witnesses are located in or near [Transferee District]. [ROA.__.] The Fifth Circuit has held that the convenience of witnesses grows more compelling as the distance between the chosen forum and the witnesses' location increases, and that once the distance exceeds 100 miles, the inconvenience grows in proportion to the additional distance. *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 204–05; *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 317. Here, [__] of the [__] identified non-party witnesses reside more than 100 miles from the courthouse chosen by Plaintiff, but within the subpoena power of the transferee court. [ROA.__.] By contrast, Plaintiff has identified no material witness or source of proof in the chosen forum. A forum with no meaningful connection to the evidence is not "clearly" the more convenient one. *See Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 316–18.

*Local interest.* The events giving rise to this suit occurred in [Transferee District], and the injury and conduct at issue implicate that community's interests. [ROA.__.] Jury service should not be imposed on citizens of a district with no relationship to the controversy. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 317–18; *Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 206.

*Remaining factors.* Neither court-congestion concerns nor familiarity with governing law favors the chosen forum. At most these factors are neutral, and a neutral factor cannot offset the weight of the private-interest factors. *See Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 289–90.

#### C. The district court's contrary reasoning rested on legal error.

The district court's denial rested on impermissible considerations. First, it relied on Plaintiff's choice of forum. But that choice is not a distinct factor in the § 1404(a) analysis. It is relevant only because it places the burden on the movant to show the transferee forum is clearly more convenient. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 314–15 & n.10. Defendant carried that burden. Treating the choice as an independent thumb on the scale is legal error.

Second, the court gave undue weight to [judicial economy / the location of counsel / the parties' general connections to the forum]. [ROA.__.] The Fifth Circuit has rejected such reasoning where it displaces the statutory convenience factors. *Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 290. Convenience of counsel is likewise irrelevant to the analysis. *See Volkswagen I*, 371 F.3d at 206.

Third, the court discounted the 100-mile rule and the location of the evidence by relying on modern technology and the ability to transport documents electronically. That reasoning would nullify the first private-interest factor. *See Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 316.

This case is unlike those in which the Fifth Circuit has left a denial of transfer undisturbed because the factors were genuinely balanced or the movant made only a thin showing. *See In re Horseshoe Entm't*, 337 F.3d 429, 432–34 (5th Cir. 2003); *cf. Weber v. PACT XPP Techs., AG*, 811 F.3d 758, 766–67 (5th Cir. 2016). Here the private-interest factors uniformly favor transfer, no factor favors the chosen forum, and the denial rested on considerations the law does not permit. Where a district court's ruling "clearly" misapplies the factors in this way, the denial is a clear abuse of discretion. *Volkswagen II*, 545 F.3d at 318–19; *Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 290; *see also In re Rolls Royce Corp.*, 775 F.3d 671, 674–75 (5th Cir. 2014).

The denial of transfer should be reversed, and the case should be remanded with instructions to transfer it to [Transferee District].
